reading.body:
Skybox Houston One does not publish its power consumption, making it impossible to determine its capacity relative to other Texas data centers or whether it hosts AI workloads.

The facility occupies 96,129 square feet across a 20-acre private campus near Houston with technical specifications suited to dense compute. It can sustain loads up to 1,000 watts per square foot using immersion cooling and withstand winds exceeding 190 mph. These are engineering choices for resilience and power density. Without a published megawatt figure, however, the facility cannot be ranked within Texas's 389 MW of disclosed capacity or compared to the 13 other Texas facilities that do disclose.

Operator transparency about power consumption varies widely. Only 13 of Texas's 133 mapped data centers publish capacity figures to this site. Skybox Houston One's silence on this metric reflects a deliberate choice by the operator, not the absence of a power infrastructure. The LEED certification covers building efficiency and environmental standards, not uptime guarantees, redundancy, or workload type.

Whether this facility serves general enterprise workloads, GPU clusters for AI training, or inference infrastructure cannot be determined from public sources. The technical design suggests it could handle any of these. The absence of a power figure is the binding constraint on understanding its role in the state's compute footprint.
